numericals.trap: External quantum efficiency and absence of internal gain are assumed.

traps.wrong: A laser is directional because stimulated emission is directional.
traps.recovery: Stimulated emission supplies coherent gain into modes; cavity geometry, aperture, and mode selection set beam direction/divergence.

traps.wrong: Interference and diffraction are unrelated phenomena.
traps.recovery: Both are superposition; diffraction is often interference across a continuous finite aperture.

traps.wrong: Higher magnification always means better resolution.
traps.recovery: Separate display scale from optical PSF, aperture, aberrations, sampling, and SNR.

traps.wrong: Uncertainty in interference is just poor alignment.
traps.recovery: Coherence, bandwidth, source size, polarization, vibration, detector averaging, and noise all matter.

traps.wrong: Total internal reflection means no field exists in the second medium.
traps.recovery: An evanescent field penetrates the lower-index medium even though no net propagating normal power exists in the ideal case.

traps.wrong: At Brewster angle there is no reflected light.
traps.recovery: Only ideal p-polarized reflection vanishes; s polarization and nonideal media remain.

traps.wrong: Rayleigh resolution is an absolute fundamental wall.
traps.recovery: Name the pupil/source/SNR/criterion; it is a conventional diffraction criterion.

traps.wrong: Population inversion alone guarantees lasing.
traps.recovery: Net modal gain must exceed internal and output-coupling losses with feedback and mode overlap.

traps.wrong: A narrow spectrum automatically proves coherence and single mode.
traps.recovery: Instrument resolution, line shape, phase noise, longitudinal/transverse modes, and measurement method matter.

traps.wrong: Quantum efficiency and responsivity are the same.
traps.recovery: QE is carriers per photon; responsivity is electrical output per optical power and depends on photon energy and gain.

speak.30: Optics needs three linked descriptions: rays for paraxial imaging, waves for phase, diffraction, interference and polarization, and photons for emission and detection. I state the approximation and geometry, then connect the observable—image, fringe, spectrum, power or current—to calibration, noise, and a limitation.
speak.90: Ray optics is the short-wavelength approximation used for refraction and imaging; it requires a sign convention and paraxial conditions. Wave optics adds amplitude and phase, so it explains coherence, interference, diffraction, polarization, and the aperture limit on resolution. A finite aperture spreads the angular spectrum, while mutually coherent paths create a stable cross term. Lasers require an inverted gain medium plus cavity feedback and mode selection; stimulated emission alone does not explain the final beam. Detection converts photons to charge, but quantum efficiency, responsivity, dark current, read noise, bandwidth, dynamic range, calibration, and saturation determine useful performance. In an interview I end each formula with its assumptions and a measurable failure mode.
speak.180: Start from electromagnetic waves and boundary phase matching. Explain Snell’s law and when geometrical optics is valid, then define optical path and paraxial imaging. Move to field superposition: interference intensity includes amplitude balance and mutual coherence, while a finite aperture produces diffraction. Derive the single-slit sinc-squared pattern and connect aperture to angular resolution, but state that Rayleigh is a criterion under a model. Treat polarization as transverse field behavior; use Malus’s law and birefringent retardance only with stated input and ideal elements. For lasers, distinguish spontaneous and stimulated emission, population inversion, cavity feedback, longitudinal/transverse modes, threshold, gain saturation, linewidth, and safety. For detectors, define QE, responsivity, dark/read/shot noise, bandwidth and dynamic range. Connect these to star sensors, remote sensing, electro-optics, spectroscopy, fibres, and astronomy, always including calibration, atmosphere/stray light, thermal stability, and the fact that magnification is not resolution.
speak.300: Use the three-minute explanation, derive the single-slit pattern or laser threshold, solve one detector or resolution estimate, and defend an optical instrument for a mission. State one approximation, one limiting case, one calibration, and one failure mode without notes.

Thermodynamics.reviewScope: Laws, processes, entropy, potentials, Maxwell relations, phase equilibrium, engines, refrigeration, numerical answers, and derivations reviewed under an explicit work-sign convention
Thermodynamics.oneMinuteCore: Thermodynamics describes equilibrium states, energy transfer, and the direction and limits of macroscopic processes. In this sheet heat added to the system is positive and work done by the system is positive, so dU=δQ−δW. Internal energy and entropy are state functions; heat and work are path-dependent transfers. The first law is energy accounting, while the second law introduces entropy generation and forbids complete conversion of cyclic heat input into work. Reversible processes are ideal limits with no entropy generation; quasistatic alone is not enough. Thermodynamic potentials are Legendre transforms chosen for controlled variables: U(S,V,N), H(S,P,N), F(T,V,N), and G(T,P,N). A spontaneity criterion is valid only under its stated constraints and says nothing by itself about reaction rate.

definitions.definition: The chosen matter/region and its separating surface; boundary may allow energy and/or matter transfer depending on the model.
A property determined by equilibrium state, so its differential is exact and its change is path independent.
Energy transferred across a boundary because of a temperature difference; it is not a substance stored in a body.
Organized energy transfer associated with generalized force–displacement variables; boundary work is only one form.
A process slow enough to pass through states arbitrarily close to equilibrium; it can still be irreversible through friction, viscosity, finite gradients, or hysteresis.
An ideal process that can be reversed with system and surroundings restored and no net entropy generation.
A state function satisfying dS=δQ_rev/T for a reversible path and ΔS_universe≥0 for an isolated total system.
H=U+PV, useful when pressure is controlled and for steady-flow energy accounting; ΔH=Q_p only under suitable conditions.
F=U−TS; at fixed T,V,N a closed system tends toward lower F until equilibrium under the allowed processes.
G=H−TS; at fixed T,P,N with only appropriate work modes, equilibrium minimizes G.
Partial molar Gibbs free energy μ_i=(∂G/∂N_i)_{T,P,N_j}; it controls matter transfer and phase/reaction equilibrium.
Energy/enthalpy response to temperature under specified constraints, e.g. C_V=(∂U/∂T)_V and C_P=(∂H/∂T)_P.
Heat transferred reversibly per amount during first-order phase change at coexistence temperature/pressure, associated with entropy discontinuity.
A quantity distinguishing phases, often tied to symmetry; its behavior depends on transition class.
Desired heat transfer divided by work input for a refrigerator or heat pump; it can exceed one without violating energy conservation.

derivations.title: Carnot efficiency from reservoir entropy balance
assumptions: Two reservoirs at T_H and T_C
Heat Q_H absorbed and Q_C rejected as positive magnitudes
Working substance returns to initial state
steps: Over one cycle ΔU=0, so W=Q_H−Q_C.
Reversibility gives zero total entropy generation.
Reservoir entropy changes sum to −Q_H/T_H+Q_C/T_C=0.
Thus Q_C/Q_H=T_C/T_H.
Efficiency η=W/Q_H=1−Q_C/Q_H=1−T_C/T_H.
derivations.interpretation: Any irreversible engine generates entropy, requiring greater heat rejection for the same input and therefore lower efficiency.
derivations.unitCheck: Temperature ratio and efficiency are dimensionless; temperatures must be absolute.
derivations.commonMistake: Using Celsius or claiming Carnot describes a practical engine’s detailed cycle.
derivations.panelInterruption: Why can COP exceed one while efficiency cannot exceed one?
derivations.summary: Use first-law cyclic energy balance and reversible reservoir entropy balance to eliminate Q_C/Q_H.

derivations.title: Maxwell relations from thermodynamic potentials
assumptions: Potentials are state functions with continuous mixed second derivatives
Composition fixed for the displayed relations
steps: Write dU=T dS−P dV, so T=(∂U/∂S)_V and −P=(∂U/∂V)_S.
Equality of mixed derivatives gives (∂T/∂V)_S=−(∂P/∂S)_V.
Legendre transform H=U+PV gives dH=T dS+V dP and (∂T/∂P)_S=(∂V/∂S)_P.
F=U−TS gives dF=−S dT−P dV and (∂S/∂V)_T=(∂P/∂T)_V.
G=H−TS gives dG=−S dT+V dP and (∂S/∂P)_T=−(∂V/∂T)_P.
derivations.interpretation: Exactness converts derivatives of entropy into measurable PVT response functions, but only under the variables held fixed.
derivations.unitCheck: Check each pair: for example (∂S/∂V)_T and (∂P/∂T)_V both have J/(m³K).
derivations.commonMistake: Memorizing signs without writing the differential and natural variables.
derivations.panelInterruption: What fails at a first-order coexistence discontinuity?
derivations.summary: Write each potential differential, identify conjugate derivatives, and equate mixed partials.

derivations.title: Clapeyron equation at phase coexistence
assumptions: Two phases α and β in equilibrium
steps: At coexistence g_α(T,P)=g_β(T,P).
Move along the coexistence line: dg_α=dg_β.
For one mole dg=−s dT+v dP.
Therefore −s_αdT+v_αdP=−s_βdT+v_βdP.
Rearrange dP/dT=Δs/Δv=Δh/(TΔv), using reversible latent heat Δh=TΔs.
derivations.interpretation: The slope sign/magnitude depends on entropy and volume changes; water’s melting line can have negative slope because liquid water is denser than ice near coexistence.
derivations.unitCheck: Δh/(TΔv) has J/mol divided by K·m³/mol = Pa/K.
derivations.commonMistake: Using the ideal-vapor Clausius approximation for solid–solid or liquid–solid transitions.
derivations.panelInterruption: Under what assumptions does this become integrated Clausius–Clapeyron?
derivations.summary: Differentiate equality of molar Gibbs energies along coexistence and substitute dg=−s dT+v dP.

rapidQuestions.a: Heat names boundary energy transfer; after transfer the energy contributes to state properties such as U.
Quasistatic stays near equilibrium; reversible additionally has no dissipative entropy generation and restores surroundings.
Adiabatic means no heat transfer; isentropic means constant entropy. Reversible adiabatic is isentropic, but irreversible adiabatic need not be.

rapidQuestions.q: What does the first law say?
rapidQuestions.a: Energy is conserved; it does not determine process direction or maximum efficiency.

rapidQuestions.q: What does the second law add?
rapidQuestions.a: Entropy generation and direction/limits of spontaneous processes and cyclic heat-to-work conversion.
For equilibrium states, dS=δQ_rev/T along a reversible path; actual entropy balances include transfer and nonnegative generation.
Yes, if sufficient entropy leaves; total entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease.

rapidQuestions.q: Why is entropy not simply disorder?
rapidQuestions.a: Disorder is an imprecise analogy; use thermodynamic definition, multiplicity/probability model and constraints.
H=U+PV, a state function useful under pressure control and in flow systems.
For a closed process at constant pressure with only PV work and compatible kinetic/potential assumptions.

rapidQuestions.a: S,V,N_i for a simple multicomponent compressible system.
T,V,N_i.
T,P,N_i.
Partial molar Gibbs free energy and conjugate to particle number; it controls matter transfer/equilibrium.
No net spontaneous heat transfer between systems in allowed contact; common temperature under the model.

rapidQuestions.a: At constant pressure heating also drives expansion work; C_P−C_V=nR for total ideal-gas capacities.
η_C=1−T_C/T_H for a reversible engine between absolute-temperature reservoirs.
Yes; it is heat moved per work input, not work output divided by heat input.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can a quasistatic piston process still be irreversible?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Friction, viscosity, finite pressure difference, inelastic deformation or hysteresis can generate entropy even through near-equilibrium states.

intermediateQuestions.q: Explain free expansion of an ideal gas.
intermediateQuestions.outline: Into vacuum: W=0; insulated Q=0; ΔU=0 and ideal-gas T unchanged, yet entropy increases because expansion is irreversible.

intermediateQuestions.q: How do you choose the correct thermodynamic potential?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Identify controlled natural variables and allowed work/matter exchange; U for S,V, F for T,V, H for S,P, G for T,P under simple assumptions.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why does ΔG<0 not guarantee a fast reaction?
intermediateQuestions.outline: G gives direction under fixed T,P constraints; activation barriers, transport, nucleation and mechanisms determine rate.

intermediateQuestions.q: How does irreversibility reduce engine efficiency?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Entropy generation increases required rejected heat for given reservoir temperatures/heat input, reducing cyclic work.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can C_P diverge near a transition?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Large fluctuations/response and nonanalytic free energy near criticality; finite-size/measurement-rate effects round real peaks.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you determine latent heat from DSC?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Calibrated baseline-subtracted peak integration per amount under controlled rate/atmosphere, repeats and separation from reaction/decomposition.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can heating and cooling transitions differ?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Nucleation barrier, kinetic lag, metastability, thermal gradients and instrument response cause hysteresis; equilibrium transition requires careful extrapolation.

intermediateQuestions.q: How does chemical potential drive diffusion?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Gradients in μ, not concentration alone, provide thermodynamic driving force; mobility/kinetics and coupled fields set flux.

intermediateQuestions.q: What changes in an open-system first law?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Add enthalpy carried by mass flow plus kinetic/potential energy, shaft work and heat under a stated control-volume convention.

deepQuestions.q: Can entropy be defined away from equilibrium?
deepQuestions.outline: Equilibrium entropy is well-defined by state; local-equilibrium or statistical/coarse-grained nonequilibrium entropies require explicit model and may not be unique.

deepQuestions.q: Why are Maxwell relations experimentally useful?
deepQuestions.outline: They replace difficult entropy derivatives with PVT/magnetic/etc response derivatives, but require equilibrium, correct held variables and smooth potential.

deepQuestions.q: Design a thermal model for a small satellite.
deepQuestions.outline: Define nodes, view factors, solar/albedo/planetary inputs, internal power, radiation εσAT⁴, conduction/contact, eclipse transient, coatings/heaters, uncertainty, validation and worst cases.

deepQuestions.q: How would you distinguish equilibrium phase stability from synthesis kinetics?
deepQuestions.outline: Use free-energy/chemical-potential expectation, vary time/rate/temperature, anneal/quench, repeat, characterize phase/composition and test metastability/transformations.

deepQuestions.outline: Audit system boundary, all energy/matter flows, reservoir temperatures at transfer, transient storage, work definition, calibration and uncertainty; a valid cyclic two-reservoir device cannot exceed the reversible bound.

speak.30: Thermodynamics separates state from process. Internal energy and entropy are state functions; heat and work are transfers. The first law conserves energy, the second law constrains direction through entropy generation, and the useful potential depends on controlled variables. Every criterion needs its assumptions.
speak.90: I use heat into the system and work by the system as positive, so dU=δQ−δW. Heat and work depend on path; U, H, F, G and S are state functions. Quasistatic does not guarantee reversible: friction or finite gradients can still generate entropy. The second law says an isolated total entropy cannot decrease. Legendre transforms choose useful natural variables: F for T,V and G for T,P. Thus ΔG≤0 is a spontaneity criterion only for a closed system at fixed T and P with appropriate work modes, and it says nothing about speed. Carnot efficiency follows from energy balance plus zero entropy generation and is an upper bound, not a practical engine model.
speak.180: Begin by define system, boundary, equilibrium and sign convention. Write dU=δQ−δW_by and explain why δQ and δW are inexact while dU is exact. Distinguish isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isochoric paths, then distinguish quasistatic from reversible. Introduce entropy through dS=δQ_rev/T and the general entropy balance with nonnegative generation. Derive Carnot efficiency using reservoir entropy balance. Then present U, H, F and G with natural variables and obtain a Maxwell relation from mixed derivatives. Explain chemical potential and coexistence, deriving Clapeyron for a phase boundary. End with applications: thermal control, synthesis and metastability, cryogenics and energy devices. For every equation state fixed variables, total versus molar units, ideal-gas assumptions and whether the result predicts equilibrium or rate.
speak.300: Use the three-minute version, derive Carnot efficiency or Clapeyron on a board, solve one work/entropy estimate, and analyze one irreversible process. Include one spacecraft or synthesis application, one limiting case, and one measurement limitation without notes.

Basic Electronics and Instrumentation.reviewScope: Lumped circuits, semiconductor devices, amplifiers, feedback, filters, sampling, conversion, sensors, noise, grounding, measurement practice, derivations, and numerical answers reviewed
Basic Electronics and Instrumentation.oneMinuteCore: Electronics turns physical signals into measurable, processable information. Start with the lumped-circuit approximation, Kirchhoff laws, energy storage, and impedance. Semiconductor devices are nonlinear and require an operating point; small-signal models are local approximations around that bias. An ideal op-amp with negative feedback is a model, not a device law: real circuits are limited by supply rails, input/output range, gain-bandwidth, slew rate, noise, bias current, offset, loading, and stability. Sampling preserves a band-limited signal only when aliasing is prevented before conversion. Instrumentation answers must include sensor principle, signal chain, calibration, uncertainty, noise bandwidth, grounding/shielding, dynamic range, drift, and failure behavior—not only a circuit diagram.

derivations.title: RC charging from Kirchhoff’s law
steps: Write KVL: V_s=v_R+v_C=Ri+C voltage.
Use i=C dv_C/dt: RC dv_C/dt+v_C=V_s.
Solve homogeneous part v_h=K e^(−t/RC) and particular v_p=V_s.
Apply v_C(0)=V_0, so K=V_0−V_s.
Obtain v_C=V_s+(V_0−V_s)e^(−t/RC).
derivations.interpretation: After one τ the remaining error is e⁻¹; the capacitor voltage cannot jump in the ideal finite-current model.
derivations.commonMistake: Assuming τ uses any visible resistor rather than the Thevenin resistance seen by the capacitor.
derivations.panelInterruption: What changes if the source has resistance or the oscilloscope probe loads the node?
derivations.summary: KVL plus i=C dv/dt gives a first-order equation with exponential approach to final voltage.

derivations.title: Ideal inverting op-amp gain
assumptions: Infinite open-loop gain in stable negative feedback
Output not saturated and bandwidth adequate
steps: Set inverting-node voltage approximately zero by virtual short.
Input current is i_in=(V_i−0)/R_in.
No current enters op-amp input, so the same current flows through R_f toward output.
KCL: V_i/R_in+(V_o/R_f)=0.
Therefore V_o/V_i=−R_f/R_in.
derivations.interpretation: Feedback drives output so summing-junction error is small; the result fails when real limits are exceeded.
derivations.commonMistake: Calling the inverting node a real ground capable of supplying current, or ignoring common-mode/output range.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do bias currents and finite gain change the result?
derivations.summary: Use virtual short plus zero input current, apply KCL at the summing node, and obtain the resistor-ratio gain.

derivations.title: Closed-loop gain and desensitivity
assumptions: Feedback signal βV_o subtracted from source
Frequency dependence suppressed until final discussion
steps: Error is e=V_s−βV_o.
Forward block gives V_o=Ae=A(V_s−βV_o).
Collect output terms: V_o(1+Aβ)=AV_s.
Thus A_cl=V_o/V_s=A/(1+Aβ).
For |Aβ|≫1, A_cl≈1/β and fractional sensitivity to A is reduced by approximately 1/(1+Aβ).
derivations.interpretation: Negative feedback can stabilize gain and improve linearity/bandwidth, but loop phase can turn it effectively positive and cause ringing or oscillation.
derivations.unitCheck: A, β and loop gain Aβ are dimensionless.
derivations.commonMistake: Saying negative feedback always improves stability without checking frequency-dependent loop phase and margins.
derivations.panelInterruption: Why does closed-loop bandwidth often increase as gain decreases for a dominant-pole op-amp?
derivations.summary: Write error subtraction and forward gain, solve algebraically, then take the large-loop-gain limit.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can an oscilloscope change the circuit being measured?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Probe resistance/capacitance, ground lead inductance, bandwidth, termination, common-mode and source impedance load the node.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you choose an RC filter for a sensor?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Define signal band, interference/alias requirement, source/load impedance, settling, noise bandwidth, tolerance, ADC drive and phase delay.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can a diode I–V sweep show hysteresis?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Self-heating, traps, capacitance, series resistance, device damage, sweep rate, measurement compliance or real material memory.

intermediateQuestions.q: How does negative feedback affect distortion and noise?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Loop gain can reduce distortion/internal error contributions inside loop, but resistor/input/source noise and bandwidth trade-offs remain; output noise requires full model.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why does capacitive load destabilize an op-amp?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Adds pole/phase lag to loop, reducing phase margin; isolation resistor/compensation or suitable device may be needed.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you detect aliasing experimentally?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Change sample rate, inspect anti-alias settings, inject known tone, compare analog spectrum, observe folded frequency dependence.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can averaging fail to improve a measurement?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Drift, 1/f/correlated noise, systematic bias, clipping, aliasing and changing measurand do not average as independent zero-mean noise.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you calibrate a temperature sensor?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Reference thermometer/bath, multi-point up/down cycles, stabilization, self-heating, placement gradients, fit/residuals, uncertainty and range.

intermediateQuestions.q: What determines ADC effective number of bits?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Measured noise/distortion/SINAD, reference, clock jitter, input driver, bandwidth, layout and test signal—not nominal code width alone.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you troubleshoot a noisy amplifier?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Check supply/grounding, termination, bandwidth, shielding, source, oscillation/clipping, component noise, layout, spectral signature and substitute known inputs.

deepQuestions.q: When does the lumped-circuit model fail?
deepQuestions.outline: Circuit dimensions comparable to wavelength/rise-time propagation, distributed transmission-line effects, radiation/coupling and reference nonuniformity; estimate delay versus timescale.

deepQuestions.q: Design a low-noise photodiode front end.
deepQuestions.outline: Photodiode mode/capacitance/current, transimpedance gain, op-amp current/voltage noise, feedback R/C stability, bandwidth, shot/dark noise, saturation, shielding, bias, calibration and ADC.

deepQuestions.q: How would you prove a sensor detects the target rather than environment?
deepQuestions.outline: Blank/control/selectivity tests, cross-sensitivity matrix, randomized exposures, calibration, drift, blind analysis, independent method and mechanism.

deepQuestions.q: How do feedback and sampling interact in a digital control loop?
deepQuestions.outline: Plant/sensor/ADC delay, sample/hold, computation, actuator, quantization, discrete poles/zeros, aliasing and stability margins.

deepQuestions.q: What would falsify a claimed 16-bit measurement?
deepQuestions.outline: Noise/ENOB, reference instability, INL/DNL, source/driver, grounding, thermal drift or calibration uncertainty much larger than one LSB; nominal codes do not prove information.

speak.30: Electronics is a signal chain from sensor to decision. I state the device/circuit model, bias and operating range, derive the transfer or time response, then check loading, bandwidth, noise, grounding, calibration, ADC limits and failure behavior.
speak.90: I begin with the lumped-circuit model, Kirchhoff laws and energy-storage elements. Semiconductor devices are nonlinear, so bias establishes an operating point and small-signal models are local. An op-amp with negative feedback approximately follows resistor-defined gain only while loop gain is high, feedback is stable and input/output, supply, bandwidth, slew and load limits are satisfied. Filters define signal and noise bandwidth and must precede an ADC to prevent aliasing. ADC bit count is not accuracy; reference, INL, DNL, noise, timing and calibration matter. For sensors I report sensitivity, selectivity, range, drift, hysteresis, response time and uncertainty, then show how grounding, shielding and test controls protect the measurement.
speak.180: Start with KCL/KVL and the declared passive sign convention. Explain R, C and L in time and frequency domains; derive RC response. Move to the p–n junction and transistor bias, emphasizing model regimes. For op-amps, derive inverting gain from virtual short and zero input current, then list real limits: common-mode, output swing/current, gain-bandwidth, slew rate, offset, bias current, noise and phase margin. Explain negative feedback through A/(1+Aβ), including instability risk. Then cover filters, anti-aliasing, ADC/DAC concepts, quantization and ENOB. Finish with instrumentation: sensor/transduction, low-noise front end, calibration, residuals, dynamic range, cross-sensitivity, grounding/shielding, fault testing and uncertainty. Connect to payload electronics, radar, radiation detectors and characterization instruments.
speak.300: Use the three-minute explanation, derive RC or op-amp gain, solve one ADC/noise estimate, and design a sensor signal chain. State operating range, calibration, bandwidth, alias protection, noise sources, grounding, uncertainty and one failure test without notes.

Mathematical Foundations, Data, and Unce.reviewScope: Units, vector calculus, linear algebra, differential equations, transforms, probability, fitting, numerical checks, uncertainty propagation, and worked answers reviewed
Mathematical Foundations, Data, and Unce.oneMinuteCore: Mathematical physics is not formula decoration; it translates assumptions into predictions and checks whether an answer can be true. Begin with dimensions, units, scales, coordinate system, symmetry, and boundary/initial conditions. Vectors and operators describe fields; linear algebra turns coupled systems into modes and eigenproblems; differential equations encode local laws; transforms separate scales or convert derivatives into algebra. Data analysis must separate a measurement, its model, calibration, random variation, systematic effects, covariance, and model inadequacy. A best fit is not automatically a true mechanism, and an uncertainty is not just the spread of repeats. Every numerical result needs units, significant figures justified by uncertainty, a limiting-case check, and a residual or convergence test where appropriate.

definitions.definition: Physical type such as mass, length, time, current, or temperature, independent of unit choice.
Agreed magnitude used to express a quantity, such as metre or electronvolt; units can change while dimensions do not.
A scalar is invariant under coordinate rotations; a vector has magnitude/direction and transforms according to the vector rule.
Vector of steepest local increase of a scalar field; directional derivative along unit u is u·∇f.
Local net outward flux density of a vector field.
Local circulation/rotation density of a vector field, with orientation by right-hand rule.
Nonzero v satisfying Av=λv; transformation preserves its direction up to scaling λ.
Measure of sensitivity of a problem/solution to perturbations under stated norm; large condition number can amplify data error.
Constraint on solution at spatial boundary; different physical boundaries select different solutions/modes.
Representation of a function in spatial/temporal frequency components under a stated convention.
Variation that changes unpredictably across repeated observations under repeatability conditions.
Recognizable effect that shifts results through calibration, method, environment, model, or selection; repeats alone need not reveal/remove it.
Joint variation measure Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−μ_X)(Y−μ_Y)]; it controls correlated uncertainty propagation.
Probability model for observed data as a function of model parameters; it is not the probability that a parameter is true.
Observed minus model-predicted value under a sign convention; residual structure diagnoses missing model behavior, dependence, or variance assumptions.

equations.conditions: Function/distribution must permit transform; normalization conventions vary.

equations.name: Mean, variance, covariance
equations.meaning: Location, spread, and joint variation.

equations.name: Poisson distribution
equations.meaning: Independent events at constant rate in fixed interval.
equations.conditions: Independence/stationary rate/no pile-up; background and dead time can violate model.

equations.name: Gaussian density

equations.name: First-order uncertainty propagation

equations.name: Weighted mean
equations.meaning: Inverse-variance weighting gives more weight to more precise independent estimates.

equations.name: Ordinary least-squares line
equations.meaning: Minimizes unweighted vertical squared residuals.
equations.conditions: x treated known, independent equal-variance zero-mean residuals for standard inference; fitting does not establish causation.

equations.name: Reduced chi-square
equations.meaning: Compares residual scale with stated independent Gaussian uncertainties.
equations.conditions: Interpret only with correct model, uncertainties, independence and degrees of freedom; near one is not proof of truth.

equations.meaning: Uncertainty of sample mean from independent identically distributed finite-variance observations.
equations.conditions: Not total measurement uncertainty; correlation, drift and systematic effects invalidate simple scaling.

derivations.title: First-order uncertainty propagation with covariance
steps: Write x_i=μ_i+δx_i and expand y=f(x)≈f(μ)+Σ_i f_i'δx_i.
Subtract mean to first order: δy≈Σ_i f_i'δx_i.
Square: δy²≈Σ_iΣ_j f_i'f_j'δx_iδx_j.
Take expectation to obtain Var(y)≈Σ_iΣ_j f_i'f_j'Cov(x_i,x_j).
For independent inputs off-diagonal covariances vanish, giving quadrature sum.
derivations.interpretation: Correlation can increase or decrease combined uncertainty; blindly adding independent terms can be wrong.
derivations.unitCheck: Each derivative product times covariance has units y².
derivations.commonMistake: Adding percentage uncertainties linearly or ignoring shared calibration correlations.
derivations.panelInterruption: When would Monte Carlo propagation be preferable?
derivations.summary: Linearize the output around input means, then propagate the covariance matrix through the gradient.

derivations.title: Ordinary least-squares slope and intercept
steps: Define S(a,b)=Σ[y_i−a−bx_i]².
Set ∂S/∂a=−2Σ(y_i−a−bx_i)=0, giving a=ȳ−b x̄.
Set ∂S/∂b=−2Σx_i(y_i−a−bx_i)=0.
Substitute a and center variables.
Solve b=Σ(x_i−x̄)(y_i−ȳ)/Σ(x_i−x̄)² and then a=ȳ−b x̄.
derivations.interpretation: The line is an optimization result under a loss/model; uncertainty and causal meaning need additional assumptions.
derivations.unitCheck: Slope has y/x units and intercept y units.
derivations.commonMistake: Using ordinary least squares when x uncertainty is important or interpreting R² as causation.
derivations.panelInterruption: How would heteroscedastic or correlated errors change the fit?
derivations.summary: Minimize squared vertical residuals, solve the two normal equations, and express them using centered data.

derivations.title: Fourier derivative property
assumptions: f and derivative sufficiently well behaved
Boundary term vanishes or distributions handled correctly
steps: Transform derivative: ∫f'(x)e^(−ikx)dx.
Integrate by parts with u=e^(−ikx), dv=f' dx.
Boundary term [f e^(−ikx)]_{−∞}^{∞} vanishes under assumption.
Remaining integral is ik∫f(x)e^(−ikx)dx.
Therefore Fourier{f'}=ikF(k), and higher derivatives multiply by (ik)^n.
derivations.interpretation: Differential equations become algebraic in frequency/wavenumber space, while boundary/initial information still matters.
derivations.unitCheck: k has inverse-length units, so ikF has derivative-transform units.
derivations.commonMistake: Forgetting transform convention sign/2π factors or boundary terms.
derivations.panelInterruption: What happens for a discontinuity or finite interval?
derivations.summary: Integrate the derivative transform by parts; differentiation becomes multiplication by ik.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Differential equation has continuum solutions, but only discrete parameters satisfy both domain boundary constraints.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Ill-conditioning amplifies perturbation; solve systems/decompose, scale, inspect singular values and uncertainty rather than explicit inverse.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Histogram/Q-Q, tails/outliers, residual versus fitted/time, independence, variance structure and domain physics; do not rely on one test.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Underestimated uncertainties dominate, correlations/heterogeneity violate weights, and measurements may target different measurands.

intermediateQuestions.q: How do you handle an outlier?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Check transcription/instrument/protocol, predefine criterion, analyze with/without transparently, use robust model, never delete for desired result.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Denominator near zero, nonlinearity, asymmetry and correlation make first-order Gaussian approximation poor; use full/Monte Carlo distribution.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Predictive performance, residuals, complexity, physical assumptions, uncertainty, preregistered criteria and independent data; not R² alone.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Versioned code/environment, inputs/seeds, units, solver/settings, tests, convergence, data provenance and documented workflow.

deepQuestions.outline: Not by repetition alone; more data may reveal drift but calibration/model/design/independent method is required, and precision can improve around wrong value.

deepQuestions.q: Design a defensible analysis for conflicting characterization methods.
deepQuestions.outline: Align measurand/sampling scale, calibrations, uncertainty/covariance, preparation, model assumptions, residuals and heterogeneity; design discriminating measurement.

deepQuestions.outline: Predefine parameter/limit predictions, test new range/data, inspect residual structure and unit/limit behavior; a flexible fit on same data is not enough.

speak.30: I start every quantitative answer with units, scale, symmetry and boundary conditions. I distinguish model from data, random spread from systematic effects, and fit quality from physical truth. I finish with uncertainty, residual or convergence check, and a limiting case.
speak.90: Mathematical physics converts a local law and boundary conditions into a testable prediction. Vector calculus describes fields and flux; linear algebra finds modes; differential equations describe evolution; Fourier methods separate scales. Before calculating I check dimensions and order of magnitude. For data I define the measurand, calibration and model, then separate random variation, systematic effects and covariance. A least-squares line is only the optimizer for a stated error model; R² is not causation. Uncertainty propagation needs derivatives and correlations, while nonlinear problems may require Monte Carlo. I report units, justified significant figures, residuals and a physical limiting case.
speak.180: Begin with dimensional homogeneity and explain why it is necessary but insufficient. Define gradient, divergence and curl and connect Gauss/Stokes to flux/circulation. Explain eigenvalues as natural modes and warn about conditioning. Show how ODEs require initial conditions and PDEs require physical boundary conditions. Fourier transform turns derivatives into ik factors and convolution into multiplication, but convention and boundary behavior matter. In data analysis, define probability model, likelihood, mean/variance/covariance, and when Gaussian or Poisson assumptions apply. Derive first-order covariance propagation. For fitting, state which variable has uncertainty, inspect residuals and avoid causal claims. Distinguish SD, SE and total measurement uncertainty. End with numerical convergence, unit tests, order-of-magnitude checks, transparent outlier treatment and reproducibility.
speak.300: Use the three-minute explanation, derive covariance propagation or least squares, solve one vector/statistics estimate, and critique a fit. Include units, covariance, residuals, significant figures, limiting case and numerical convergence without notes.

Classical Mechanics and Oscillations.reviewScope: Newtonian, rotating-frame, Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, central-force, oscillation, wave, experimental and numerical content reviewed
Classical Mechanics and Oscillations.oneMinuteCore: Classical mechanics predicts motion from forces or, more generally, from variational and Hamiltonian structure. First define the system, frame, coordinates, constraints, and force model. Newton’s laws apply directly in inertial frames; accelerating or rotating coordinates require inertial-force terms with signs derived from the acceleration transformation. Conservation laws follow from isolation and symmetry, not because energy or momentum are always conserved. Lagrangian mechanics handles generalized coordinates and ideal constraints; Hamiltonian mechanics moves to phase space, but the Hamiltonian equals total energy only under suitable conditions. Oscillations near a stable equilibrium are approximately harmonic because the potential is locally quadratic. Damping, driving, coupling, dispersion, and nonlinearities determine real response, resonance, energy flow, and failure of simple models.

definitions.definition: A frame in which a free particle moves with constant velocity and Newton’s second law holds without inertial-force corrections.
Restriction on allowed configurations or velocities; holonomic constraints can be written as relations among coordinates and time.
Independent parameter describing configuration after constraints, not necessarily a Cartesian length.
Line integral of force along displacement in the chosen frame; only the component along displacement contributes.
Force derivable from a single-valued potential over the relevant domain, with path-independent work under stated conditions.
Mass-weighted position R=(Σm_i r_i)/M; its acceleration is set by net external force.
L=r×p about a specified origin; its time derivative equals torque with origin/frame qualifications.
In rotating coordinates, inertial force −2mΩ×v_rot acting on motion relative to the rotating frame.
Function L(q,q̇,t), often T−V, whose stationary action yields equations of motion for an appropriate model.
Generalized coordinate absent explicitly from L; its conjugate momentum is conserved.
Legendre transform H=Σp_iq̇_i−L when transformation is regular; generator of canonical time evolution.
Space of generalized coordinates and conjugate momenta; one system state is a point in it.
Equilibrium for which sufficiently small perturbations remain bounded; positive quadratic potential curvature is a local one-dimensional criterion.
Collective oscillation pattern in which all coordinates vary at one eigenfrequency with fixed amplitude ratios.
Dependence of angular frequency on wavevector; it separates phase and group velocities and can reshape pulses.

equations.name: Newton’s second law
equations.meaning: Net external force changes momentum in an inertial frame.
equations.conditions: State system/frame; variable-mass systems require momentum-flux treatment rather than naive m dv/dt alone.

equations.name: Work-energy theorem
equations.meaning: Net work changes kinetic energy.
equations.conditions: Particle/inertial-frame form; include constraints, deformable bodies and frame choice appropriately.

equations.name: Linear momentum balance
equations.meaning: Internal action-reaction forces cancel under the model, leaving external force for total momentum.
equations.conditions: Closed particle system with suitable internal-force symmetry; fields/flux may carry momentum.

equations.name: Angular momentum balance
equations.meaning: External torque changes angular momentum.
equations.conditions: Inertial origin or include moving-origin terms; define particle/body system.

equations.name: Rigid-body rotation about fixed principal axis
equations.symbols: I moment of inertia about axis
equations.meaning: Rotational analog under fixed-axis assumptions.
equations.conditions: Rigid body and fixed principal axis; general rotation uses tensors and Euler equations.

equations.name: Rotating-frame acceleration
equations.meaning: Relates inertial acceleration to relative, Coriolis, centrifugal and Euler terms.
equations.conditions: r measured from moving origin; signs of fictitious forces are negative of extra acceleration terms in m a_R equation.

equations.name: Euler–Lagrange equation
equations.meaning: Stationary-action equations for independent variations.
equations.conditions: Appropriate L, ideal/handled constraints and fixed endpoint variations.

equations.name: Hamilton equations
equations.meaning: First-order phase-space evolution.
equations.conditions: Regular Legendre transform; H need not equal energy for time-dependent coordinates/potentials.

equations.name: Central-force effective potential
equations.meaning: Radial motion becomes one-dimensional with centrifugal barrier.
equations.conditions: Time-independent central force, reduced one-body description and planar motion.

equations.name: Small oscillation
equations.meaning: Quadratic potential gives sinusoidal motion.
equations.conditions: Small displacement, linear restoring force, constant parameters, negligible damping/driving.

equations.name: Damped oscillator
equations.meaning: Underdamped motion decays at rate β and oscillates at ω_d.
equations.conditions: Linear viscous damping; underdamped when β<ω₀.

equations.name: Driven response amplitude
equations.meaning: Steady-state amplitude peaks near resonance with damping-dependent frequency/width.
equations.conditions: Linear steady state after transient; displacement resonance is not exactly ω₀ when damping finite.

equations.name: Quality factor
equations.meaning: Measures stored energy relative to loss per radian/cycle convention and relates to resonance width.
equations.conditions: Linear weakly damped oscillator; define bandwidth/energy convention.

equations.name: Phase and group velocities
equations.meaning: Phase fronts and narrowband envelope propagate differently in dispersive media.
equations.conditions: Group velocity envelope interpretation requires narrow bandwidth and care in loss/anomalous dispersion.

derivations.title: Work-energy theorem
assumptions: Net force includes all modeled forces
steps: Start with F=m dv/dt.
Dot with velocity v=dr/dt: F·v=m(dv/dt)·v.
Recognize m v·dv/dt=d(½mv²)/dt.
Integrate over time: ∫F·v dt=K₂−K₁.
Use v dt=dr to obtain ∫F·dr=ΔK.
derivations.interpretation: Only net force work changes kinetic energy; conservative-force work can be moved into potential energy.
derivations.commonMistake: Using one force’s work as total work or ignoring frame-dependent kinetic energy/work.
derivations.panelInterruption: Does a static normal force always do zero work?
derivations.summary: Dot Newton’s law with velocity and integrate; power from net force is time derivative of kinetic energy.

derivations.title: Euler–Lagrange equation from stationary action
assumptions: Allowed variation q→q+εη with η endpoints zero
Constraints already incorporated or treated separately
steps: Compute first variation δS=∫[(∂L/∂q)η+(∂L/∂q̇)η̇]dt.
Integrate the η̇ term by parts.
Endpoint term vanishes because η(t₁)=η(t₂)=0.
Then δS=∫[∂L/∂q−d/dt(∂L/∂q̇)]η dt.
Arbitrary η requires the bracket vanish, giving d/dt(∂L/∂q̇)−∂L/∂q=0.
derivations.interpretation: Dynamics follow stationary—not necessarily minimum—action; generalized coordinates automatically respect incorporated constraints.
derivations.unitCheck: Each Euler–Lagrange term has generalized-force units.
derivations.commonMistake: Saying nature chooses the path with minimum L at every instant or forgetting fixed endpoint variation.
derivations.panelInterruption: How are nonconservative generalized forces included?
derivations.summary: Vary the action, integrate velocity variation by parts, use fixed endpoints, and invoke arbitrary coordinate variation.

derivations.title: Effective potential for central-force motion
assumptions: Potential V(r) depends only on radius
steps: Write L=½m(ṙ²+r²φ̇²)−V(r).
φ is cyclic, so p_φ=mr²φ̇=ℓ is constant.
Energy is E=½m ṙ²+½m r²φ̇²+V(r).
Replace φ̇=ℓ/(mr²).
Obtain E=½m ṙ²+[V(r)+ℓ²/(2mr²)] and identify V_eff.
derivations.interpretation: Turning points satisfy E=V_eff; circular orbits are extrema of V_eff and stability depends on second derivative.
derivations.commonMistake: Treating centrifugal barrier as a new physical central force without stating reduced radial description.
derivations.panelInterruption: What conditions make a circular orbit stable?
derivations.summary: Use angular-momentum conservation to eliminate angular speed and rewrite energy as radial kinetic plus effective potential.

intermediateQuestions.outline: If point of application moves along force—moving boundary/elevator/rolling contact—work may occur; static horizontal surface case is special.

intermediateQuestions.q: How does changing origin affect angular momentum?
intermediateQuestions.outline: L_O shifts by R×P; torque relation gains moving-origin terms unless origin inertial/COM conditions.

intermediateQuestions.outline: External torque small so angular momentum Iω conserved; internal work changes rotational kinetic energy.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Set dV_eff/dr=0; stability requires second derivative positive; apply to gravitational V=−GMm/r.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why is centrifugal force derivable from a potential for constant Ω?
intermediateQuestions.outline: −mΩ×(Ω×r) corresponds to gradient of −½m|Ω×r|² under constant frame rotation; Coriolis is velocity-dependent.

intermediateQuestions.q: How do constraints simplify Lagrangian mechanics?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Choose independent generalized coordinates so ideal constraint forces need not appear; nonholonomic/time-dependent constraints require care.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can Hamiltonian be conserved when coordinate momenta change?
intermediateQuestions.outline: If ∂H/∂t=0 total H is conserved while canonical variables exchange energy; conservation is not each momentum.

intermediateQuestions.outline: Damping/Q in linear model, plus finite observation, drive noise, inhomogeneity and nonlinearity.

deepQuestions.outline: Depends on time dependence of rotating-frame L/H and potentials; for constant Ω an effective conserved quantity may exist, while physical inertial-frame energy differs.

deepQuestions.outline: Continuous action symmetry gives conserved current/quantity: time translation energy, spatial translation momentum, rotation angular momentum, with boundary/gauge qualifications.

deepQuestions.q: Why can resonance destroy a structure if the forcing is weak?
deepQuestions.outline: Coherent energy accumulation over many cycles when loss low; finite Q, mode shape, stress concentration, nonlinear saturation and fatigue.

deepQuestions.q: Design a model hierarchy for spacecraft attitude motion.
deepQuestions.outline: Rigid body Euler equations, inertia tensor, external torques, wheels/magnetorquers, sensors, linearization near attitude, flexible modes, disturbances, control and validation.

deepQuestions.outline: Frequency depends on amplitude, waveform harmonics, asymmetric potential, nonexponential damping, mode coupling or residual structure beyond uncertainty.

traps.recovery: Momentum and energy have different conditions; internal energy can increase.

traps.wrong: Angular momentum is conserved because an object rotates.
traps.recovery: Require zero net external torque about specified origin.

traps.wrong: Centrifugal force is a fundamental interaction.
traps.recovery: It is an inertial term in rotating coordinates; derive sign from acceleration transform.

traps.wrong: Lagrangian is always T−V.
traps.recovery: T−V is common for natural conservative systems; velocity-dependent potentials, fields and constraints can modify form.

traps.wrong: Hamiltonian always equals total energy.
traps.recovery: State regular transform and time-independent natural-coordinate conditions.

traps.wrong: Resonance always occurs exactly at ω₀.
traps.recovery: Peak depends on damping, observable and model; displacement peak shifts with damping.

traps.wrong: High Q is always good.
traps.recovery: High Q increases selectivity/sensitivity but slows settling and raises resonant vulnerability.

traps.wrong: Group velocity always equals signal or energy velocity.
traps.recovery: Only under suitable narrowband/weak-loss conditions; anomalous/absorbing media require care.

speak.30: In mechanics I first define system, frame, coordinates, constraints and forces. I choose Newton, energy, momentum or Lagrangian method, state conservation conditions, and check units and limiting cases. For oscillations I identify equilibrium, linear range, damping, drive, modes and resonance limits.
speak.90: Newton’s laws apply directly in inertial frames, so a free-body diagram must isolate one system and include every external force. Work-energy handles displacement, impulse-momentum handles short interactions, and angular-momentum conservation requires zero external torque about a stated origin. In rotating frames I derive Coriolis, centrifugal and Euler terms from acceleration transformation. Lagrangian mechanics uses generalized coordinates and stationary action; cyclic coordinates give conserved momenta. Hamiltonian mechanics uses phase space, but H is not always total energy. Near stable equilibrium the potential is quadratic, giving SHM; real systems add damping, driving, coupling, nonlinear response and dispersion.
speak.180: Start with the system and inertial frame. State ΣF=dp/dt, derive work-energy, and distinguish conditions for momentum, angular momentum and mechanical-energy conservation. For central forces, zero torque makes motion planar and effective potential turns the radial problem into one dimension; circular orbits are extrema and stability uses curvature. For rotating frames, write the full acceleration transformation before assigning inertial-force signs. Then derive Euler–Lagrange from stationary action and explain generalized/cyclic coordinates. Introduce Hamilton equations and the conditions under which H is energy. For oscillations, expand potential near equilibrium, define ω₀, damping β, driven amplitude, phase, Q and normal modes. End with experiments, residuals, nonlinear limits, spacecraft or vibration applications and uncertainty.
speak.300: Use the three-minute explanation, derive Euler–Lagrange or effective potential, solve one collision/orbit/oscillator estimate, and diagnose a resonance experiment. Include frame, origin, constraints, conservation conditions, damping and one failure of linear theory without notes.

Electromagnetic Theory.reviewScope: Electrostatics, magnetostatics, materials, Maxwell equations, boundary conditions, waves, energy, conductors, antennas, numerical answers and derivations reviewed
Electromagnetic Theory.oneMinuteCore: Electromagnetism is a field theory linking charges and currents to electric and magnetic fields. Electrostatics uses Gauss’s law and a scalar potential when curl E is zero; magnetostatics uses steady currents, Biot–Savart/Ampère laws and a vector potential. Maxwell’s displacement-current term makes charge continuity consistent and allows coupled electric and magnetic fields to propagate as waves. Boundary conditions come from integral Maxwell equations and depend on free surface charge/current plus material constitutive laws. Electromagnetic energy flows through the Poynting vector and can be stored, transmitted, reflected, absorbed or dissipated. Every answer must distinguish E from D, B from H, free from bound sources, field from potential, phase from energy flow, and ideal vacuum/linear media from dispersive, lossy, anisotropic real materials.

prerequisites.why: Gradient, divergence, curl, Gauss and Stokes theorems are Maxwell’s mathematical language.
Poisson/Laplace/wave equations need geometry and boundary conditions.

Polarization, magnetization, conductivity, permittivity and permeability are constitutive responses.
E, D, B, H, flux, potential, impedance and energy-density units are frequent traps.

definitions.definition: Force per unit test charge in the limiting sense, including electric part of Lorentz force; units V/m or N/C.
Scalar whose electrostatic difference gives work per charge and E=−∇V in curl-free regions; reference is arbitrary.
Auxiliary field with ∇·D=ρ_free under the chosen macroscopic split; D=ε₀E+P.
Electric dipole moment per unit volume; spatial variation creates bound charge.
Field entering magnetic Lorentz force qv×B and Faraday flux; units tesla.
Auxiliary macroscopic field H=B/μ₀−M with curl tied to free current plus displacement term.
Magnetic dipole moment per unit volume; can be represented by bound currents under macroscopic model.
Potentials can change by transformations leaving E and B unchanged; potentials are not unique.
ε₀∂E/∂t in vacuum form, or ∂D/∂t in macroscopic Ampère–Maxwell law; it is a field term, not necessarily material charge crossing a gap.
S=E×H, electromagnetic energy-flux density in common macroscopic formulation.
Ratio of transverse electric to magnetic field amplitudes for a specified mode/medium, complex in lossy media.
Distance over which field amplitude falls by e in a good conductor under harmonic steady state.
State of transverse electric-field orientation/evolution; distinct from material polarization P.
Angular distribution of radiated power/intensity in a stated far-field plane or solid angle.
Regions where reactive/source-size terms dominate versus radiative angular field with approximately transverse 1/r behavior; boundary depends on wavelength and aperture size.

equations.meaning: Inverse-square electrostatic field.
equations.conditions: Point/static charge, vacuum, superposition; real distributions require integration and material boundaries.

equations.name: Electrostatic potential
equations.meaning: Potential converts electrostatic field to scalar boundary-value problem.
equations.conditions: Electrostatics; in charge-free region ∇²V=0.

equations.meaning: Charge sources electric flux; no observed magnetic monopole source in Maxwell theory.
equations.conditions: Integral forms handle distributions/surfaces; macroscopic D uses free charge.

equations.name: Biot–Savart law
equations.meaning: Magnetostatic field from current element.
equations.conditions: Steady localized current; full time-dependent fields require retarded solutions/Maxwell equations.

equations.name: Faraday law
equations.meaning: Changing magnetic flux is linked to circulating electric field.
equations.conditions: Moving/deforming circuits require motional EMF qv×B contribution and careful flux rule.

equations.name: Ampère–Maxwell law
equations.meaning: Current and changing electric field source magnetic curl.
equations.conditions: Macroscopic media commonly use ∇×H=J_free+∂D/∂t.

equations.name: Vacuum wave equations
equations.meaning: Maxwell equations support transverse waves.
equations.conditions: ρ=0, J=0, homogeneous vacuum; sources/boundaries add inhomogeneous terms.

equations.name: Poynting theorem
equations.meaning: Local electromagnetic energy conservation.
equations.conditions: Material dispersion/loss requires careful energy definitions; J·E is power transferred to matter.

equations.name: Boundary conditions
equations.meaning: Normal/tangential jumps follow pillbox/loop Maxwell integrals.
equations.conditions: No impulsive time-varying surface flux for displayed E tangential form; orientations/signs stated.

equations.name: Parallel-plate capacitance
equations.meaning: Geometry/material store electric energy.
equations.conditions: Neglect fringing, linear nondispersive dielectric for simple energy density.

equations.name: Good-conductor skin depth
equations.meaning: Harmonic field amplitude decays over δ and phase advances similarly.
equations.conditions: Good conductor σ≫ωε, homogeneous linear medium.

equations.name: Friis free-space relation
equations.meaning: Ideal free-space link scaling.
equations.conditions: Line of sight, far field, no multipath/atmosphere/mismatch; gains and losses consistently defined.

derivations.title: Electromagnetic wave equation from Maxwell equations
steps: Start with ∇×E=−∂B/∂t.
Use identity ∇×(∇×E)=∇(∇·E)−∇²E and ∇·E=0.
Use ∇×B=μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t.
Obtain ∇²E−μ₀ε₀∂²E/∂t²=0, so speed c=1/√(μ₀ε₀).
derivations.interpretation: Coupled time-varying E and B propagate without local sources; boundary/source conditions select actual solutions.
derivations.unitCheck: Both terms have E-field per m² units because μ₀ε₀ has s²/m².
derivations.commonMistake: Setting divergence E to zero without stating source-free region or claiming all EM waves are plane waves.
derivations.panelInterruption: How does the equation change in a conducting medium?
derivations.summary: Curl Faraday, substitute Ampère–Maxwell, use vector identity and source-free divergence.

derivations.title: Poynting theorem
steps: Dot E with Ampère–Maxwell: E·(∇×B)/μ₀=J·E+ε₀E·∂E/∂t.
Dot B/μ₀ with Faraday: (B/μ₀)·(∇×E)=−(B/μ₀)·∂B/∂t.
Rearrange to ∇·(E×B/μ₀)+∂[½ε₀E²+B²/(2μ₀)]/∂t=−J·E.
Identify S=E×B/μ₀ and field energy density u.
derivations.interpretation: Decrease of field energy plus outward flux equals work done by fields on charges; energy can flow through space around a circuit.
derivations.commonMistake: Treating S as energy density rather than flux, or ignoring sign of J·E.
derivations.panelInterruption: Where does energy flow when charging a capacitor?
derivations.summary: Combine dotted curl equations with the divergence identity to obtain local field-energy conservation.

derivations.title: Electromagnetic boundary conditions
assumptions: Interface with unit normal from medium 1 to 2
Fields finite near interface except allowed surface sources
steps: Apply ∮D·dA=Q_free to pillbox: n·(D₂−D₁)=σ_f.
Apply ∮B·dA=0: n·(B₂−B₁)=0.
Apply Faraday to vanishing rectangular loop; finite dΦ_B/dt vanishes with area, yielding n×(E₂−E₁)=0.
Apply Ampère–Maxwell to loop; displacement area term vanishes while surface free current remains, yielding n×(H₂−H₁)=K_f.
Combine with constitutive laws only after stating medium model.
derivations.interpretation: Maxwell equations constrain jumps; constitutive response determines field values/reflection/refraction.
derivations.unitCheck: D jump C/m² and H jump A/m match surface sources.
derivations.commonMistake: Saying normal E or tangential B is always continuous regardless of material/surface sources.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do these produce Fresnel reflection?
derivations.summary: Use pillboxes for normal components and shrinking loops for tangential components, retaining allowed surface charge/current.

limitingCases.boundary: Superconductors/perfect conductors differ magnetically; real conductors have finite skin depth and transients.

rapidQuestions.a: E is force per charge; electrostatic V is scalar energy per charge with E=−∇V.

rapidQuestions.q: When is electric potential globally useful?
rapidQuestions.a: Electrostatic/curl-free E in appropriate domain; time-varying E generally also needs vector potential.
Local charge-source density through ∇·E=ρ/ε₀ in microscopic vacuum form.
Local circulation; Faraday law links it to changing B.

rapidQuestions.q: Why is field inside electrostatic conductor zero?
rapidQuestions.a: Mobile charges redistribute until no field drives steady interior current in equilibrium.

rapidQuestions.q: Can a cavity in conductor contain field?
rapidQuestions.a: Empty shielded cavity without enclosed charge is field-free electrostatically under conditions; enclosed charges/boundaries can create field.
Geometry/material-dependent proportionality Q=CV for a specified two-conductor configuration in linear regime.
Polarization reduces field/potential difference for given free charge under common geometry, increasing Q/V.
Time-derivative electric-flux term that completes Ampère law and continuity; not necessarily charge crossing dielectric gap.
Maxwell theory has no magnetic monopole source; magnetic field lines form closed/divergence-free flux.

rapidQuestions.q: Does magnetic force do work on a point charge?
rapidQuestions.a: qv×B is perpendicular to v, so instantaneous magnetic power is zero; fields can still exchange energy through induced E/material systems.
B=∇×A; A has gauge freedom and contributes to E through −∂A/∂t.
Transform potentials without changing E and B; choose gauge for convenience while observables remain invariant.
Charge sources electric divergence; magnetic divergence zero; changing B curls E; current/changing E curl magnetic field.

rapidQuestions.q: Why are vacuum plane waves transverse?
rapidQuestions.a: Source-free divergence conditions give k·E=k·B=0, while curl equations link perpendicular fields.
c=1/√(μ₀ε₀) from Maxwell wave equation.
Electromagnetic energy flux density S=E×H in common macroscopic formulation.
Momentum transfer per area/time from electromagnetic radiation; depends on absorption/reflection and geometry.
E/H amplitude ratio for a specified mode/medium, possibly complex.
Boundary conditions plus impedance/wavevector mismatch require reflected and transmitted fields.
Receiver/antenna responds to projection of incident polarization; mismatch reduces coupled power.
Amplitude e-folding penetration distance in a conductor for harmonic field.

rapidQuestions.q: Why does skin depth decrease with frequency?
rapidQuestions.a: In good conductor δ∝1/√(ωμσ), as induction confines current near surface.
Near field includes reactive/source-geometry terms; far field is predominantly radiative/transverse with stable angular pattern.
Directivity is angular concentration relative isotropic; gain includes radiation efficiency.

rapidQuestions.q: Why can antenna aperture improve gain?
rapidQuestions.a: Larger effective aperture at fixed wavelength supports narrower beam/higher directivity under efficiency/illumination limits.
Geometric spreading relation between isotropic-equivalent transmit and receive aperture/gain, not dissipative loss of vacuum.
Dispersive plasma refraction, delay, absorption/scintillation depend on frequency, path and activity.
Absorption, scattering, refraction, rain/cloud and turbulence affect propagation by frequency.
Power density transferred from electromagnetic field to charges/matter; sign can reverse locally.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can E normal jump at dielectric interface?
intermediateQuestions.outline: D normal jump set by free surface charge; E=D/ε in linear media, so ε contrast changes E even with σ_free=0.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can H tangential jump?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Free surface current K_f appears in Ampère boundary condition; B/H constitutive response also matters.

intermediateQuestions.q: How does displacement current preserve charge continuity?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Take divergence of Ampère–Maxwell; divergence curl zero plus Gauss yields ∇·J+∂ρ/∂t=0.

intermediateQuestions.q: Where does energy enter a charging capacitor?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Poynting flux flows through surrounding space into gap/field energy, with source doing work and resistive loss as applicable.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you distinguish conduction and displacement current?
intermediateQuestions.outline: J_cond=σE material transport; ∂D/∂t field/polarization term; both contribute to magnetic curl and can be complex/frequency dependent.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why does a wave attenuate in conductor?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Induced currents dissipate J·E; complex propagation constant gives decay and phase, with skin depth in good-conductor limit.

intermediateQuestions.q: How do boundary conditions lead to Snell’s law?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Phase continuity along interface conserves tangential wavevector, yielding n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂ in isotropic media.

intermediateQuestions.q: Why can group and phase velocities differ?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Material/waveguide dispersion makes ω(k) nonlinear; v_p=ω/k, v_g=dω/dk; loss complicates energy velocity.

intermediateQuestions.q: How would you measure an antenna pattern correctly?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Far-field distance, reference antenna/power, alignment/polarization, rotation, dynamic range, multipath control and normalization.

intermediateQuestions.q: What limits Friis equation use?
intermediateQuestions.outline: Far-field line-of-sight, impedance/polarization match, known gains, no multipath/atmosphere and consistent system losses.

deepQuestions.q: Are E and B frame invariant?
deepQuestions.outline: No; relativistic transformations mix them. Lorentz force/Maxwell equations are covariant and electric/magnetic split depends on observer.

deepQuestions.q: How should electromagnetic energy be defined in dispersive media?
deepQuestions.outline: Simple ½E·D+½B·H may fail; account frequency dispersion, loss and microscopic/material energy with a stated model.

deepQuestions.q: Can Poynting vector point opposite phase velocity?
deepQuestions.outline: In negative-index/anisotropic/guided media energy flow, wavevector and phase can differ; distinguish S, k, group and energy velocity.

deepQuestions.q: Design EMC validation for a spacecraft sensor.
deepQuestions.outline: Define susceptibility/emission paths, grounding/bonding, cable/shield, conducted/radiated tests, frequency/power levels, calibration, functional criteria and fault margins.

deepQuestions.q: What would falsify a claimed shielding improvement?
deepQuestions.outline: Calibrated insertion loss fails across relevant frequency/geometry/polarization, leakage seams dominate, sensor floor/normalization error, repeat configurations and near/far-field differences.

speak.30: Electromagnetism links sources to fields through Maxwell equations. I distinguish E,D,B,H and free/bound sources, derive boundary or wave behavior from integral/differential laws, and finish with energy flow, material assumptions and a measurable limitation.
speak.90: Electrostatics has ∇·E=ρ/ε₀ and curl E=0, so E=−∇V and Poisson/Laplace equations become boundary-value problems. Steady currents source magnetic curl, while Faraday induction and Maxwell displacement current couple time-varying E and B and enforce charge continuity. In source-free vacuum they produce transverse waves at c=1/√(μ₀ε₀). Boundary conditions constrain normal D/B and tangential E/H with free surface charge/current. Poynting theorem tracks field energy, flux and J·E work. Real applications then require constitutive laws, dispersion, loss, skin depth, impedance, polarization, antenna pattern and calibration.
speak.180: Start by define microscopic versus macroscopic fields and source split. Present four Maxwell equations in differential and integral meaning. For electrostatics use potential, Poisson/Laplace, conductor and dielectric boundaries; for magnetostatics use Lorentz, Biot–Savart, Ampère and vector potential. Explain why displacement current is needed by taking divergence and recovering continuity. Derive the vacuum wave equation and plane-wave E,B,k relation. Derive Poynting theorem to show energy flows through fields and into matter via J·E. Obtain boundary conditions with pillboxes/loops before applying ε,μ,σ. Then discuss reflection, polarization, impedance, conductors/skin depth, near/far fields, antennas and link budgets. Connect to satellite communications, radar, remote sensing, EMC, sensors and materials, always stating frequency, geometry, calibration and loss model.
speak.300: Use the three-minute explanation, derive the wave equation or Poynting theorem, solve one field/wave/skin-depth estimate, and defend one interface or antenna measurement. Include source region, boundary conditions, constitutive law, units and one failure of an ideal model without notes.

Quantum Mechanics.reviewScope: Foundations, formalism, one-dimensional systems, tunnelling, oscillator, angular momentum, spin, identical particles, approximations, experiments, numericals and derivations reviewed
Quantum Mechanics.oneMinuteCore: Quantum mechanics represents a physical preparation by a state vector or wavefunction, not by a classical trajectory. The state predicts outcome probabilities through the Born rule. Observables are represented by self-adjoint operators with domains and boundary conditions; measurement outcomes and probabilities follow their spectral structure. Between measurements an isolated state evolves unitarily by the Schrödinger equation. Superposition is linear at amplitude level, so relative phase matters. Uncertainty follows noncommuting observables and state spread, not merely poor apparatus. Stationary states have time-independent probability density but a time-dependent global phase. Tunnelling does not violate energy conservation: an energy eigenstate can have nonzero transmission through a classically forbidden region. Every solution must state Hilbert space, Hamiltonian, boundary conditions, normalization, approximation and what is actually measured.

definitions.definition: A ray in Hilbert space representing a preparation; normalized vectors differing only by global phase represent the same pure state.
State amplitude in a chosen basis, e.g. ψ(x)=⟨x|ψ⟩; it is not directly a classical material wave.
Probability density for position is |ψ(x)|², and more generally outcome probability is given by projection/POVM rule.
Physical quantity represented ideally by a self-adjoint operator or more generally a measurement operator framework.
Ensemble mean predicted for repeated identically prepared measurements, ⟨A⟩=⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩.
[A,B]=AB−BA; it encodes compatibility, dynamics and uncertainty relations.
Energy eigenstate whose time evolution is a phase e^(−iEt/ħ), leaving time-independent expectation of time-independent observables.
Two or more independent states share an eigenvalue, often due to symmetry.
Spatial inversion symmetry; in one dimension parity eigenvalues are ±1 for symmetric potentials.
j=(ħ/m)Im(ψ*∇ψ) for the standard Schrödinger particle; with density it satisfies continuity.
Nonzero transmission/amplitude through a region classically forbidden at the same total energy.
Intrinsic angular momentum with no classical rigid-body interpretation; spin-½ has two outcomes along any axis.
Particles of same species whose labels are not physical observables; many-body state is symmetric for bosons and antisymmetric for fermions.
Controlled expansion around a solvable Hamiltonian when perturbation is sufficiently small relative to relevant gaps/matrix elements.
For normalized trial state, expectation of H is at least ground-state energy; quality depends on trial family.

derivations.title: Infinite square-well eigenstates and energies
steps: Inside, time-independent Schrödinger equation is −(ħ²/2m)ψʺ=Eψ.
For E>0 write ψ=A sin kx+B cos kx with k²=2mE/ħ².
Boundary ψ(0)=0 gives B=0.
Boundary ψ(L)=0 requires sin(kL)=0, so kL=nπ with n positive integer.
Normalize A=√(2/L) and obtain E_n=ħ²k²/(2m)=n²π²ħ²/(2mL²).
derivations.interpretation: Quantization comes from wave equation plus confinement boundary conditions; n=0 would give zero wavefunction, not a state.
derivations.commonMistake: Allowing n=0 or saying particle literally follows standing-wave trajectory.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do finite walls alter boundary conditions and spectrum?
derivations.summary: Solve sinusoidal interior equation, impose two zero boundaries, normalize, and read discrete k and E.

derivations.title: Robertson uncertainty relation
assumptions: A and B self-adjoint on appropriate domains
steps: Define centered operators Ã=A−⟨A⟩ and B̃=B−⟨B⟩.
Cauchy–Schwarz gives ⟨Ã²⟩⟨B̃²⟩≥|⟨ÃB̃⟩|².
Split ÃB̃=½{Ã,B̃}+½[Ã,B̃].
For self-adjoint A,B, anticommutator expectation is real and commutator expectation imaginary.
Dropping nonnegative anticommutator contribution yields ΔAΔB≥½|⟨[A,B]⟩|.
derivations.interpretation: Bound concerns state spreads of repeated measurements, not only apparatus disturbance.
derivations.unitCheck: Commutator expectation has product units AB.
derivations.commonMistake: Writing ΔxΔp=ħ/2 as equality for every state.
derivations.panelInterruption: Which states saturate position–momentum bound?
derivations.summary: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to centered operator states and isolate commutator contribution.

derivations.title: Exponential tunnelling factor through a rectangular barrier
assumptions: Thick-barrier/WKB leading exponential; prefactor not derived
steps: Inside forbidden region Schrödinger equation gives ψʺ=κ²ψ with κ=√[2m(V₀−E)]/ħ.
Solutions are growing/decaying exponentials e^{±κx}.
Across a sufficiently opaque barrier, amplitude reaching far side is suppressed roughly by e^{−κa}.
Transmission probability is amplitude squared, giving leading factor T∝e^{−2κa}.
Exact matching supplies an energy-dependent prefactor and preserves probability current.
derivations.interpretation: Barrier width and energy deficit enter exponentially; transmitted particles retain total energy E in stationary elastic model.
derivations.commonMistake: Calling e^{−2κa} exact for every barrier or claiming particle borrows energy.
derivations.panelInterruption: Why must ψ and ψ′ be matched for finite potential step?
derivations.summary: Forbidden-region wave decays with κ; crossing width a suppresses amplitude e^{−κa} and probability approximately e^{−2κa}.
